question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

TENACIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Persistent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tenacious (adjective) means holding firmly to something and refusing to give up; determined and persistent. (दृढ़संकल्प, डटा रहने वाला)
◦ Example: Her tenacious pursuit of the case finally forced an inquiry.

 

• Persistent carries the same sense — continuing firmly in a course of action in spite of difficulty. (लगातार प्रयास करने वाला)
◦ Example: Persistent questioning by the journalist brought the facts to light.

 

• The word comes from Latin tenere (to hold), the same root as tenant, tenure and retain. The physical sense survives in expressions such as a tenacious grip.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Yielding (नम्र, हार मान लेने वाला): giving way easily — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Fickle (चंचल, अस्थिर): changing one’s loyalties or opinions frequently — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Hesitant (हिचकिचाने वाला): slow to act through doubt.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of tenacious asked in SSC: dogged, resolute, steadfast, unwavering, pertinacious.

 

• Antonyms: irresolute, wavering, vacillating, half-hearted, capricious.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

MAGNANIMOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Petty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Magnanimous (adjective) means generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or a defeated opponent; large-hearted. (उदार, महान)
◦ Example: In a magnanimous gesture, the winner praised his opponent’s courage.

 

• Petty means small-minded, concerned with trivial matters and unwilling to be generous, and is therefore its direct opposite. (तुच्छ, संकीर्ण)
◦ Example: The dispute was reduced to a petty quarrel over seating.

 

• The word is built from Latin magnus (great) + animus (mind, spirit) — literally “great of spirit”. The same root gives magnitude, magnify and magnate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Generous (उदार): willing to give freely — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Benevolent (हितैषी, दयालु): kindly and well-meaning — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Noble (उदात्त, श्रेष्ठ): having high moral qualities — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Three options agree and one stands apart — the odd option is the answer. Other antonyms of magnanimous: vindictive, mean, miserly, spiteful, ungenerous.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

At one’s wits’ end
option_2: Utterly perplexed and unable to think what to do next
option_3: At the close of a long and tiring journey
option_4: On the point of losing one’s temper
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Utterly perplexed and unable to think what to do next.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “At one’s wits’ end” means so worried or puzzled by a difficulty that one can think of nothing further to do. (बुद्धि काम न करना, हक्का-बक्का रह जाना)
◦ Example: After three days without news of the missing boat, the families were at their wits’ end.

 

• The image is of the wits — one’s powers of reasoning — having been used up to their very end, so that no idea remains.

 

• Note that the idiom describes helpless bewilderment, not anger and not cleverness; the presence of the word wits is a deliberate trap in such questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 would be described by “to have one’s wits about one”, which means quite the reverse — to be alert and quick-thinking.

 

• Option 3 refers to physical exhaustion — “on one’s last legs”.

 

• Option 4 refers to anger — “to fly off the handle”.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of confusion and difficulty worth revising: in a fix, in deep water, between the devil and the deep sea, at a loose end (having nothing to do — not to be confused with the idiom above).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PROFUSE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Scanty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Profuse (adjective) means very plentiful, produced or given in great quantity. (प्रचुर, भरपूर)
◦ Example: He offered profuse apologies for the delay.

 

• Scanty means too small in amount, barely sufficient, and is therefore its direct opposite. (अल्प, नितांत कम)
◦ Example: The evidence was too scanty to support a conviction.

 

• The word comes from Latin profundere (to pour forth), which explains its use with things that flow or spill over — profuse bleeding, profuse praise, profuse growth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Abundant (प्रचुर): existing in large quantity — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Copious (प्रचुर, विपुल): plentiful in supply — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Lavish (उदारतापूर्वक, भरपूर): given in generous or extravagant amounts — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of profuse: meagre, sparse, scarce, paltry, exiguous. Note the useful pair profuse – profusion (noun) and scanty – scarcity.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the adjective describing a medicine that reduces fever.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Antipyretic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Antipyretic describes a drug that lowers or prevents fever. (ज्वरनाशक)
◦ Example: Paracetamol is prescribed both as an analgesic and as an antipyretic.

 

• The spelling is fixed by the Greek elements anti- (against) + pyretos (fever), from pyr — fire. The middle of the word is therefore -pyre-, with a ‘y’ followed by ‘e’, and the ending is the ordinary -tic.

 

• The same root pyr- appears in pyre, pyrotechnics (fireworks) and pyromania.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Antipyritic — the ‘e’ of pyretos has been replaced by an ‘i’.

 

• Option 3: Antipiretic — the ‘y’ of the root pyr has been lost.

 

• Option 4: Antipyrretic — the ‘r’ has been doubled without warrant.

 

NOTE

 

• Learn the drug-class adjectives together: analgesic (relieves pain), antiseptic (prevents infection), anaesthetic (removes sensation), antidote (counteracts poison), antibiotic (destroys bacteria).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitution for:

 ‘A person who believes that nothing can be known about the existence of God’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Agnostic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An agnostic is a person who holds that the existence of God is unknown and probably unknowable — the position is one of suspended judgement, not of denial. (अज्ञेयवादी)
◦ Example: He described himself as an agnostic, unwilling to affirm or deny what he could not verify.

 

• The word is built from Greek a- (not) + gnosis (knowledge) — literally “without knowledge”. The same root gives diagnosis and prognosis.

 

• The definition turns on the words “nothing can be known”; that is what separates the answer from the commonest distractor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Atheist (नास्तिक): one who denies the existence of God — a positive disbelief, not a suspension of judgement.

 

• Option 3: Fanatic (कट्टरपंथी): a person filled with excessive and uncritical zeal for a cause.

 

• Option 4: Zealot (उग्र समर्थक): an uncompromising and often intolerant supporter of a belief.

 

NOTE

 

• The related cluster is set repeatedly in SSC: theist (believes in God), deist, polytheist (believes in many gods), monotheist (believes in one god), iconoclast (one who attacks cherished beliefs), sceptic (one who habitually doubts).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

‘A formal expression of severe disapproval passed by an assembly’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Censure.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Censure means the formal expression of strong disapproval, especially by a legislature, a court or a professional body. (निंदा, भर्त्सना)
◦ Example: The house passed a motion of censure against the minister.

 

• Two elements of the definition must be satisfied together — the disapproval must be formal, and it must be expressed by a body, not by an individual. Both point to censure.

 

• Do not confuse censure (to condemn) with censor (to examine and suppress objectionable material), which differ by a single letter and are regularly set as a pair.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sanction (स्वीकृति / प्रतिबंध): a curious word with two opposed senses — official permission, and a penalty imposed to enforce a rule.

 

• Option 3: Injunction (निषेधाज्ञा): a court order requiring someone to do, or to refrain from doing, a particular act.

 

• Option 4: Impeachment (महाभियोग): the formal charging of a high public official with misconduct, which begins a process of removal.

 

NOTE

 

• Related parliamentary vocabulary: moratorium (an authorised delay), quorum (the minimum number required to transact business), veto (the power to reject), adjournment (a suspension of proceedings), ratification (formal approval).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option:

 

Not only ____ the original deadline, but he also submitted a revised estimate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. did he meet.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with ‘Not only’, the clause that follows must be inverted — it takes the question order auxiliary + subject + main verb.
◦ Complete sentence: Not only did he meet the original deadline, but he also submitted a revised estimate.

 

• Since the verb met is in the simple past and has no auxiliary of its own, the auxiliary did is supplied to carry the tense, and the main verb returns to its base form meet.

 

• The inversion is required only when the negative adverbial stands first in the sentence. In mid-position no inversion occurs: He not only met the deadline but also submitted a revised estimate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘he met’ keeps normal statement order and ignores the compulsory inversion.

 

• Option 3: ‘he did meet’ uses the emphatic did but still places the subject before the auxiliary.

 

• Option 4: ‘had he met’ is inverted but introduces the past perfect, which does not suit two actions of the same time.

 

NOTE

 

• Expressions that force inversion when placed first: Not only, Never, Seldom, Rarely, Hardly, Scarcely, No sooner, Little, Nowhere, Under no circumstances, Only then, Only after.

question:
Select the correct option:

 

The minister sought to ____ the fears of the striking workers with a promise of fresh talks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. allay.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Allay (verb) means to make a fear, doubt or suspicion less intense; to calm or relieve it. (शांत करना, कम करना)
◦ Complete sentence: The minister sought to allay the fears of the striking workers with a promise of fresh talks.

 

• The clue lies in the phrase “with a promise of fresh talks”. A conciliatory offer is made in order to reduce anxiety, not to increase it; the sentence therefore requires a verb of calming.

 

• The word collocates with a fixed set of nouns — one allays fears, doubts, suspicions, anxieties and concerns.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Aggravate (बिगाड़ना): to make a bad situation worse — the opposite of the sense required.

 

• Option 3: Arouse (जगाना, भड़काना): to awaken or stir up a feeling — one arouses suspicion rather than settling it.

 

• Option 4: Amplify (बढ़ाना): to increase in strength or volume.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs of calming set against verbs of stirring: allay, assuage, placate, mollify, appease on one side; inflame, provoke, incite, exacerbate, kindle on the other.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

Seldom does he visits the branch office (1)/ without first informing (2)/ the regional manager (3)/ about the purpose of his visit. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence opens with the negative adverb ‘Seldom’, which correctly forces the inversion does he. But once the auxiliary does has been used, the main verb must stand in its base form — visit, not visits.
◦ Corrected: Seldom does he visit the branch office without first informing the regional manager about the purpose of his visit.

 

• The rule is a general one: after do, does, did and after every modal, the verb takes V1 and never carries the -s of the third person.
◦ He visits the office. / He does not visit the office.

 

• The tense is already shown by does; repeating it on the main verb is a double marking of the present.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct: without is a preposition and rightly takes the -ing form informing.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the regional manager is the object of informing.

 

• Part (4) is correct: an ordinary prepositional phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• The same error is often set with “Little did he knew”, “Never did she wrote” or “Did he went?” In every case the cure is the same — after do/does/did, use the first form of the verb.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

Are they repairing the old suspension bridge?
option_1: Is the old suspension bridge repaired by them?
option_2: Is the old suspension bridge being repaired by them?
option_3: Has the old suspension bridge been repaired by them?
option_4: Are the old suspension bridge being repaired by them?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Is the old suspension bridge being repaired by them?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is an interrogative in the present continuous. Its passive is formed as:
◦ Is/Are + object + being + V3 + by + subject + ?

 

• Applying the rule step by step:
◦ the object the old suspension bridge becomes the subject and, being singular, takes is — not the are of the original, which agreed with they;
◦ are repairing becomes being repaired;
◦ the auxiliary stays before the subject so that the sentence remains a question, and the question mark is retained.

 

• Passive: Is the old suspension bridge being repaired by them?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 omits being and so gives the passive of the simple present (Do they repair …?).

 

• Option 3 is the passive of the present perfect (Have they repaired …?).

 

• Option 4 retains the plural are with a singular subject.

 

NOTE

 

• In the passive of a question, the auxiliary agrees with the new subject, never with the old one, and the interrogative word order must be preserved: Was he writing the letter? → Was the letter being written by him?

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

What the department needs most (1)/ are a clear set of guidelines (2)/ and a system of monitoring (3)/ that officials can actually follow. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is the noun clause ‘What the department needs most’, and such a clause is treated as singular. The verb must therefore be is, not are.
◦ Corrected: What the department needs most is a clear set of guidelines and a system of monitoring that officials can actually follow.

 

• The plural-sounding words that follow the verb — guidelines, a system — are part of the complement, not the subject, and a verb never agrees with its complement.

 

• Note also that the true head of the complement is ‘a set’, itself singular; the plural guidelines sits inside a prepositional phrase.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: needs rightly agrees with the singular the department inside the clause.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the second element of the complement is properly joined by and.

 

• Part (4) is correct: that officials can actually follow is a well-formed relative clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Subjects that always take a singular verb although they look plural: a what-clause (What we need is …), a that-clause (That they refused is odd), a gerund phrase (Reading books is useful), and an infinitive phrase (To err is human).

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The captain lost the toss shortly before the match began.
option_1: He struck a match to light the hurricane lamp.
option_2: The match was abandoned because of poor visibility.
option_3: Tickets for the final match were sold out within an hour.
option_4: The second match of the series ended in a draw.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He struck a match to light the hurricane lamp.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, match means a sporting contest between two sides. (मुकाबला)

 

• In Option 1, match means a short stick tipped with a compound that produces flame when rubbed. (माड़िस की तीली) That is a completely different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The remaining options all use match in the sense of a contest, exactly as the highlighted word does.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: the match was abandoned — a contest; identical in meaning to the given sentence.

 

• Option 3: tickets for the final match — again a contest.

 

• Option 4: the second match of the series — the same sense once more.

 

NOTE

 

• The word has a third common sense — a thing that corresponds to another (The paint was a perfect match) — and gives the idiom “to meet one’s match”, meaning to encounter an equal or a superior.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The first prize was awarded to the youngest competitor by the panel of judges.
option_1: The panel of judges awarded the first prize to the youngest competitor.
option_2: The panel of judges had awarded the first prize to the youngest competitor.
option_3: The youngest competitor was awarded the first prize.
option_4: The panel of judges have awarded the first prize to the youngest competitor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The panel of judges awarded the first prize to the youngest competitor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — the panel of judges — becomes the subject of the active sentence, and the passive subject the first prize becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb was awarded is in the simple past, so the active verb is simply awarded. The indirect object to the youngest competitor is carried over unchanged.
◦ Active: The panel of judges awarded the first prize to the youngest competitor.

 

• Note that panel is a singular collective noun here, so it takes a singular verb; the plural judges sits inside the phrase of judges.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 shifts the verb to the past perfect, which would place the award before some other past event not mentioned.

 

• Option 3 remains in the passive voice; only the order of the objects has been changed.

 

• Option 4 uses the present perfect have awarded, wrong both in tense and in agreement with panel.

 

NOTE

 

• A verb with two objects — award, give, offer, teach, send, pay — allows two passives: The prize was awarded to her and She was awarded the prize. Either may appear in the question; the active form is the same for both.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

In the discourse of progress, the opposition between tradition and innovation is habitually presented as a contest with a foregone conclusion. Tradition is cast as inertia — the accumulated weight of habit, defended by those with the least to gain from change — while innovation wears the borrowed prestige of the future. Yet the opposition is a caricature, and a costly one. A tradition is not a museum of finished objects; it is a body of solved problems, and the solutions it preserves were themselves innovations that once survived their trials. To inherit a craft, a legal code or a cropping calendar is to receive, compressed into custom, the results of experiments that no living person has the time to repeat. Innovation, for its part, is rarely the spontaneous leap of legend. It proceeds by recombination — a technique borrowed from one field and applied in another, an old form loaded with new material, a constraint accepted and then turned to advantage. The innovator who knows no tradition is condemned to rediscover, expensively, what was settled long ago; the guardian who admits no innovation preserves the form of a practice while losing the reason for which it was adopted. Each, left to itself, decays into a parody of itself: tradition into ritual observance, innovation into novelty for its own sake. What is required, then, is not a compromise struck between two rivals but the recognition that they are phases of a single process. A living tradition is one that argues with itself, testing its inheritance against conditions its founders never met and discarding what no longer holds. Cultures do not choose between the anchor and the sail; a vessel that carries only one of the two either never leaves the harbour or is never seen again.

 

Which of the following best captures the tone of the author in the passage?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Reflective.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Reflective means thoughtful, weighing a matter carefully rather than reacting to it. (चिंतनपरक)

 

• The author examines a familiar opposition, shows why it is a caricature, gives the weakness of each side in turn, and closes with a considered image rather than a verdict against anybody. Nothing is mocked, nothing is lamented, and no one is blamed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Dismissive would require the author to brush aside one of the two positions; instead both are given their due.

 

• Option 3: Sentimental suggests an appeal to emotion or nostalgia — the passage defends tradition on grounds of usefulness, not affection.

 

• Option 4: Indignant suggests anger at a wrong; the writing is measured throughout.

 

NOTE

 

• A passage that presents both sides fairly before offering a synthesis is almost always reflective or analytical in tone. Words of blame or ridicule, if absent, rule out the sharper options at once.

Select the statement that most clearly presents the limitation of relying solely on innovation.
option_1: Innovation wears the borrowed prestige of the future
option_2: Innovation proceeds by recombination rather than by sudden leaps
option_3: The innovator who knows no tradition must rediscover, at great cost, what was long ago settled
option_4: A living tradition is one that argues with itself
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The innovator who knows no tradition must rediscover, at great cost, what was long ago settled.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The question asks for a limitation — what goes wrong when innovation is pursued without tradition. Only this statement names a penalty: the wasteful repetition of work already done.

 

• The author reinforces the point immediately afterwards, saying that innovation left to itself decays into novelty for its own sake.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes how innovation is perceived by others, not a weakness in it.

 

• Option 2 describes the method by which innovation actually works; it is an observation, not a limitation.

 

• Option 4 concerns tradition, and states a virtue rather than a defect.

 

NOTE

 

• For “which statement presents the limitation” questions, test each option with a single question: does it name a cost or a failure? Statements of definition, method or perception can be eliminated at once.

Each, left to itself, decays into a parody of itself: tradition into ritual observance, innovation into novelty for its own sake. What is required, then, is not a compromise struck between two rivals but the recognition that they are phases of a single process. A living tradition is one that argues with itself, testing its inheritance against conditions its founders never met and discarding what no longer holds. Cultures do not choose between the anchor and the sail; a vessel that carries only one of the two either never leaves the harbour or is never seen again.

 

From a philosophical perspective, what argument does the author make about tradition and innovation?
option_1: One of the two must eventually replace the other
option_2: They are phases of a single process rather than rivals
option_3: They belong to entirely unrelated spheres of life
option_4: Tradition alone can secure lasting progress
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. They are phases of a single process rather than rivals.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states the position directly: what is required is not a compromise struck between two rivals but the recognition that they are phases of a single process.

 

• The whole argument prepares that conclusion — the solutions preserved by a tradition were once innovations, and innovation works by recombining what already exists. Each therefore contains the other.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 restates the very contest with a foregone conclusion that the author calls a caricature.

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by every example in the passage, all of which show the two intertwined.

 

• Option 4 takes one side; the author explicitly warns that a guardian who admits no innovation loses the reason for the practice he preserves.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage sets up an apparent opposition, the answer to a “what argument does the author make” question is usually a synthesis rather than a victory for one side. Look for the sentence beginning What is required … or In essence …

A living tradition is one that argues with itself, testing its inheritance against conditions its founders never met and discarding what no longer holds. Cultures do not choose between the anchor and the sail; a vessel that carries only one of the two either never leaves the harbour or is never seen again.

 

What does the phrase “a body of solved problems” imply about tradition?
option_1: That tradition is a record of failures best forgotten
option_2: That tradition stores the results of earlier experiments that worked
option_3: That tradition is indifferent to the problems of the present
option_4: That tradition is valued only for its beauty
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That tradition stores the results of earlier experiments that worked.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase is set against the image the author rejects — tradition as a museum of finished objects. The contrast tells us that a tradition is working knowledge, not a display of relics.

 

• The next sentence completes the meaning: the solutions a tradition preserves were themselves innovations that once survived their trials, and to inherit them is to receive the results of experiments no living person has time to repeat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the sense — what a tradition retains is precisely what succeeded.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the closing paragraph, in which a living tradition tests itself against present conditions.

 

• Option 4 revives the museum image that the author explicitly sets aside.

 

NOTE

 

• A phrase introduced by “not X; it is Y” is always explained by the contrast itself. Read the rejected image first; the meaning of the accepted one follows from it.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

In the discourse of progress, the opposition between tradition and innovation is habitually presented as a contest with a foregone conclusion. Tradition is cast as inertia — the accumulated weight of habit, defended by those with the least to gain from change — while innovation wears the borrowed prestige of the future. Yet the opposition is a caricature, and a costly one. A tradition is not a museum of finished objects; it is a body of solved problems, and the solutions it preserves were themselves innovations that once survived their trials. To inherit a craft, a legal code or a cropping calendar is to receive, compressed into custom, the results of experiments that no living person has the time to repeat. Innovation, for its part, is rarely the spontaneous leap of legend. It proceeds by recombination — a technique borrowed from one field and applied in another, an old form loaded with new material, a constraint accepted and then turned to advantage. The innovator who knows no tradition is condemned to rediscover, expensively, what was settled long ago; the guardian who admits no innovation preserves the form of a practice while losing the reason for which it was adopted. Each, left to itself, decays into a parody of itself: tradition into ritual observance, innovation into novelty for its own sake. What is required, then, is not a compromise struck between two rivals but the recognition that they are phases of a single process. A living tradition is one that argues with itself, testing its inheritance against conditions its founders never met and discarding what no longer holds. Cultures do not choose between the anchor and the sail; a vessel that carries only one of the two either never leaves the harbour or is never seen again.

 

Which metaphor does the author use for the relationship between tradition and innovation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The anchor and the sail.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage closes with the image of a vessel: cultures do not choose between the anchor and the sail, and a vessel carrying only one of the two either never leaves the harbour or is never seen again.

 

• The metaphor is exactly fitted to the argument — the anchor (tradition) prevents drift, the sail (innovation) provides movement, and each is useless without the other.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 picks up the word museum, but that image is introduced only to be rejected, and no laboratory is mentioned at all.

 

• Option 3 borrows harbour from the final sentence, where it is part of the consequence, not the metaphor itself.

 

• Option 4 is a plausible image for growth, but it appears nowhere in the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• Distractors in metaphor questions are commonly built out of words that really do occur in the passage. Check that the option names the image the author actually uses, and not a word borrowed from its surroundings.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The new recruit is quite capable to handle the additional workload.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. of handling.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective capable is always followed by of + gerund (-ing form), never by a to-infinitive.
◦ Corrected: The new recruit is quite capable of handling the additional workload.
◦ Example: The machine is capable of printing four hundred pages a minute.

 

• Contrast it with able, which takes the infinitive: He is able to handle the workload. The two adjectives are close in meaning but take opposite structures — which is precisely what this question tests.

 

• The negative forms follow the same pattern: incapable of doing, unable to do.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘for handling’ — capable does not take for; that preposition belongs with responsible, eligible, famous.

 

• Option 3: ‘to handling’ — the preposition is wrong, even though the gerund is right.

 

• Option 4: ‘in handling’ — in would suit interested or engaged, not capable.

 

NOTE

 

• Adjective + preposition pairs regularly tested: capable of, incapable of, desirous of, confident of, afraid of, addicted to, prone to, indifferent to, familiar with, popular with.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

If the driver would have applied the brakes earlier, the accident might have been avoided.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. had applied.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ‘Would’ is never used in the *if*-clause of a conditional sentence. The main clause here is might have been avoided, which marks this as a third conditional — a past situation that did not happen.

 

• The third conditional requires If + past perfect … would/could/might + have + V3, so the if-clause must read had applied.
◦ Corrected: If the driver had applied the brakes earlier, the accident might have been avoided.

 

• The same sentence may be written with inversion, dropping if: *Had the driver applied the brakes earlier …*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘would apply’ repeats the very error the question is testing.

 

• Option 3: ‘has applied’ is present perfect and cannot describe an unreal past condition.

 

• Option 4: ‘applies’ belongs to the first conditional, which would need will in the main clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the two prohibitions in conditional sentences: no ‘will’ and no ‘would’ inside the *if*-clause. The one accepted exception is a polite request — If you would kindly wait here …

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

She admitted that she had not read the report before signing it.
option_1: “I had not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.
option_2: “I did not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.
option_3: “She did not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.
option_4: “I have not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. “I did not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The past reporting verb admitted had pushed the original verb one step back. Converting to direct speech means undoing that back-shift: the past perfect had not read returns to the simple past, did not read.

 

• The pronoun she becomes I, since the speaker now speaks in her own voice, and the sentence is enclosed in inverted commas with a capital letter at the start.
◦ Direct: “I did not read the report before signing it,” she admitted.

 

• The clause before signing it contains a gerund and is unaffected by the change of speech.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the back-shifted past perfect, so no conversion has taken place.

 

• Option 3 leaves the reported pronoun she inside the quotation, which no speaker would use of herself.

 

• Option 4 uses the present perfect, which would mean she has still not read the report — a change of meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• The past perfect of reported speech may come from either the simple past or the present perfect of the original. Context decides which to restore: here before signing it fixes the action firmly in the past, so the simple past is correct.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The guard said, “The last train leaves at ten every night.”
option_1: The guard said that the last train left at ten every night.
option_2: The guard said that the last train leaves at ten every night.
option_3: The guard said that the last train had left at ten every night.
option_4: The guard said that the last train would leave at ten every night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The guard said that the last train leaves at ten every night.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The ordinary rule of back-shift has an important exception: when the reported words state a universal truth, a scientific fact, a habitual action or a fixed timetable, the tense is left unchanged, even after a past reporting verb.

 

• The words at ten every night show that this is a standing arrangement, still true at the moment of reporting. The present tense leaves** is therefore retained.
◦ Indirect: The guard said that the last train leaves at ten every night.

 

• Compare: He said, “Water boils at 100°C.” → He said that water boils at 100°C.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 applies the back-shift mechanically and suggests the timetable is no longer in force.

 

• Option 3 uses the past perfect, which turns a recurring departure into a single completed one.

 

• Option 4 turns a present fact into a future intention.

 

NOTE

 

• Tenses that stay unchanged in reported speech: universal truths (the earth revolves), habitual facts (she walks to work), timetables (the train leaves at six), and clauses of improbable or unreal condition (if I were you).

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. For nearly a century the flightless bird was known only from a single damaged skin in a distant museum.

 

A. Expeditions sent to the island in the 1930s came back with nothing more than rumours gathered from herdsmen.

 

B. Ornithologists therefore disagreed over whether the skin represented a living species at all.

 

C. A photograph taken by a shepherd in a remote valley finally settled the question.

 

D. Within a decade the bird had been located, counted and placed under legal protection.

 

S2. The species survives today in a valley of less than forty square kilometres, watched over by a permanent field station.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-A-C-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – C – D – S2, and the paragraph follows the order evidence → doubt → failed search → proof → outcome.

 

• S1 presents the sole evidence — one damaged skin.
◦ B begins with “therefore” and speaks of “the skin”, both of which point straight back to S1, so B must come first.
◦ A describes the attempts made to resolve that doubt, and their failure.
◦ C supplies the proof and says that the question was “finally settled” — a word that presupposes the long uncertainty of B and A.
◦ D records the consequence, within a decade, and leads naturally into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-C-D) sends out expeditions before any doubt has been raised, and strands the connective therefore.

 

• Option 3 (B-C-A-D) settles the question in C and then resumes a fruitless search in A.

 

• Option 4 (A-C-B-D) places the disagreement after the photograph that ended it.

 

NOTE

 

• Words such as “finally”, “at last” and “in the end” mark the close of a sequence of attempts. The sentence carrying them can never stand before the attempts it concludes.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The famous blue of old Indian cotton came from a plant that gives no blue at all.

 

A. Only after the dipped cloth was lifted into the air did it turn, within minutes, from yellow-green to deep blue.

 

B. The leaves of the indigo plant yield a colourless substance that must first be fermented in water.

 

C. The liquor that resulted was itself a murky yellow, so dyers judged their vats by smell and froth rather than by colour.

 

D. Cloth was steeped in that liquor for as long as the depth of shade demanded.

 

S2. The dye that made the fabric famous across three continents was thus never blue in the vat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-C-D-A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – C – D – A – S2, and the paragraph follows the order of the process itself: raw material → the vat → dipping → the change of colour.

 

• S1 states the paradox — a blue that comes from a plant giving no blue.
◦ B explains the raw material and the first step, fermentation.
◦ C describes “the liquor that resulted”, a phrase that can only refer to the fermentation in B.
◦ D speaks of steeping the cloth in “that liquor”, so it must follow C.
◦ A gives the final transformation, and its wording — “the dipped cloth” — presupposes the dipping described in D.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-D-C-A) dips the cloth before the vat liquor has been described.

 

• Option 2 (C-B-D-A) opens with “the liquor that resulted” before anything has resulted.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-C-A) begins in the middle of the process, with “that liquor” unexplained.

 

NOTE

 

• In a paragraph describing a process, the sentences follow the physical order of the steps. Demonstratives such as that liquor, the dipped cloth, the resulting mixture then confirm the chain, each pointing back to the step immediately before.
